Subject: Scheduling Approach for Multi-Mode, Resource-Constrained Project

Team,

This memo outlines the scheduling challenge for our current project and sets expectations for how we will plan and coordinate work under time, resource, and budget limits.

Context and scope
- The project consists of multiple activities that must be sequenced in line with defined dependencies. Each activity must be selected in exactly one execution option.
- Each execution option (mode) for an activity comes with a different duration, resource draw, and cost. Faster options are available but are more expensive.

Execution modes and trade-offs
- For each activity, we will choose one mode. Shorter modes compress the timeline but consume more budget and may use more resources; longer modes reduce cost and may reduce resource pressure but extend the schedule.
- Resources used by an activity are considered renewable: once an activity completes, its assigned resources return to the pool and can be reassigned.

Dependencies and timing constraints
- Activities are subject to precedence constraints that define what must finish before something else can start. Several of these dependencies include minimum waiting times (the successor cannot start until a lag has passed after the predecessor finishes) and, in some cases, maximum waiting times (the successor must start within a given window after the predecessor finishes).
- Some activities cannot start before a specified earliest start time (release date), and some must finish by a hard deadline.
- Activities are non-preemptive: once an activity starts, it runs continuously to completion in its chosen mode.

Resource limits and conflict handling
- We have multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity. Activities may compete for these resources based on their chosen modes.
- To protect against capacity overload under uncertainty about mode choices at the time of sequencing, we will apply a conservative safety rule: if two activities are not linked by precedence and there exists at least one pairing of their modes and at least one resource for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities must not overlap. One will be scheduled to finish before the other starts.
- This is the only resource feasibility rule we will enforce; there is no additional “at all times” capacity balancing beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions. The intent is to simplify coordination while avoiding any possibility of exceeding available resources.

Budget constraint
- There is a fixed overall project budget. The sum of the selected mode costs across all activities must not exceed this budget. This creates a direct trade-off between faster, more expensive modes and slower, less expensive ones across the portfolio of activities.

Planning goal
- Our goal is to complete all activities as early as possible by selecting modes and setting start times that respect:
  - All precedence requirements, including minimum and maximum delays;
  - All release dates and deadlines;
  - The conservative pairwise resource safety rule; and
  - The fixed overall budget.
- The outcome will be an integrated baseline schedule that minimizes total project duration (makespan) while staying within budget and honoring all timing and resource constraints.

Next steps
- We will confirm the dependency map (including any minimum and maximum lags), validate release and deadline commitments, and lock the available capacities for each resource type.
- We will then select a mode for each activity and determine the required pairwise sequencing for any non-dependent activity pairs that trigger the safety rule.
- Finally, we will align start dates to satisfy all constraints and produce the baseline schedule, with clear justifications for mode selections and sequencing decisions.
